label: Formulated the doctrine of universal hylomorphism and spiritual matter
description: Ibn Gabirol formulated the thesis that all created substances, including incorporeal intellects and souls, are composed of universal matter and universal form, distinguishing them from the absolute simplicity of God.
historicalContext: Articulated in 11th-century Muslim Andalusia (Zaragoza/Valencia), synthesizing Neoplatonism with Jewish theology.
dialecticalTension: Contrasts with the orthodox Aristotelian and Thomistic view that spiritual beings (intellects/angels) are immaterial, subsistent forms without matter.

citations.author: Solomon ibn Gabirol
citations.quote: Universal Matter and Universal Form are the foundations of all created things, both spiritual and corporeal.

citations.author: Sarah Pessin
citations.work: Ibn Gabirol's Theology of Desire: Matter and Beyond in Jewish and Islamic Neoplatonism

label: Adapted Plotinian emanation and intelligible matter
description: Ibn Gabirol drew directly on the Plotinian tradition (specifically the Enneads' doctrine of intelligible matter) to structure his cosmic hierarchy descending from the Divine Will.
historicalContext: Transmission of Neoplatonic texts into medieval Muslim and Jewish philosophy in al-Andalus.
dialecticalTension: Elevates the Divine Will (Irada/Ratzon) as a dynamic intermediary between the absolute One and universal matter, departing from Plotinus's non-volitional emanation.

citations.author: Fernand Brunner
citations.work: Métaphysique d'Ibn Gabirol et de la tradition platonicienne

label: Prompted Maimonidean critique of Neoplatonic hypostases and spiritual matter
description: Maimonides in his philosophical and rabbinic writing rejected Ibn Gabirol's universal hylomorphism, adhering strictly to Aristotelian physics and the immateriality of the separate intellects.
historicalContext: The 12th-century Andalusian transition from early Jewish Neoplatonism to classical Aristotelianism.
dialecticalTension: Pits Ibn Gabirol's Neoplatonic universal hylomorphism against Maimonides's strict Aristotelian peripateticism.

citations.author: Moses Maimonides
citations.quote: The separate intellects are incorporeal forms entirely free from matter.

citations.author: Colette Sirat
citations.work: A History of Jewish Philosophy in the Middle Ages

label: Sparked Aquinas's refutation of Avicebron's universal hylomorphism
description: Thomas Aquinas engaged extensively with Ibn Gabirol (under the Latinized name Avicebron) in 'De Ente et Essentia' and the 'Summa Theologiae', rejecting the idea that immaterial angels possess spiritual matter.
historicalContext: The 13th-century Latin Scholastic debate in Paris between Franciscan Augustinians (who embraced Gabirol) and Dominican Thomists.
dialecticalTension: Aquinas argues that angels are pure forms whose limitation comes from the distinction between essence and existence, not spiritual matter.

citations.author: Thomas Aquinas
citations.work: De Ente et Essentia (On Being and Essence)
citations.quote: Avicebron asserted in the Fons Vitae that the soul and other separate substances are composed of matter and form; but this position cannot stand.

citations.author: John M. Quinn
citations.work: The Thomism of Etienne Gilson: A Critical Study

label: Informed Spinoza's monistic conception of infinite substance and divine unity
description: Scholars of Jewish philosophy note that Ibn Gabirol's Keter Malkhut and Fons Vitae, widely studied in the Amsterdam Sephardic community, helped prefigure Spinoza's conception of a single, all-encompassing divine reality.
historicalContext: Early modern transmission of medieval Sephardic Hebrew philosophy in 17th-century Amsterdam.
dialecticalTension: Transforms Gabirol's theological pantheistic overtones and divine will into Spinoza's deterministic Deus sive Natura.

citations.author: Shlomo Pines
